AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: Little is known about how obstructive defecation and colonic inertia symptoms contribute to constipation-related quality of life.

AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: We sought to characterize the differences in quality of life in patients with severe obstructive defecation and colonic inertia symptoms.

AbstractText.Label: DESIGN
AbstractText.content: This study was a cross-sectional analysis of a prospective database.

AbstractText.Label: SETTING
AbstractText.content: Patients were enrolled at a single tertiary referral center.

AbstractText.Label: PATIENTS
AbstractText.content: We included consecutive adults with severe symptoms of obstructive defecation (n = 115) or colonic inertia (n = 90) as measured by the Constipation Severity Instrument.

AbstractText.Label: MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
AbstractText.content: The primary outcomes measured were the Pelvic Floor Distress Inventory, Constipation-Related Quality of Life instrument, Pelvic Floor Impact Questionnaire, and 12-item Short Form Health Survey.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Although physical examination and anorectal physiology testing were similar between groups, patients with severe obstructive defecation symptoms reported worse pain, distress, and constipation-specific quality of life than patients with severe colonic inertia symptoms (all p < 0.001). Specifically, patients with severe obstructive defecation symptoms showed greater quality-of-life impairment related to eating, bathroom habits, and social functioning (all p ≤ 0.01). Furthermore, patients with severe obstructive defecation symptoms had inferior global quality of life on the 12-item Short Form Health Survey physical component score (p = 0.03) and mental component score (p = 0.06).

AbstractText.Label: LIMITATIONS
AbstractText.content: The use of patient self-report instruments resulted in a proportion of patients with incomplete data.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: Quality of life was impaired in both groups of patients; however, patients with severe obstructive defecation symptoms were affected to a significantly greater extent. The fact that there were no differences in objective findings on physical examination or anorectal physiology studies highlights the importance of assessing quality of life during the evaluation and treatment of constipated patients.
